statement: For a [field](c:field) $K$ and nodes $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\in K$, the [Vandermonde matrix](c:vandermonde-determinant) $V_{ij}=a_i^j$ has $\det V=\prod_{i<j}(a_j-a_i)$. So $V$ is invertible exactly when the nodes are distinct. For distinct nodes, each data vector has exactly one [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree below $n$ with those values.

hypotheses.text: The set $K$ is a [field](c:field).
The number $n$ is a nonnegative integer.
For the interpolation claim, the nodes are pairwise distinct.

conclusion: The [determinant](c:determinant) of $V$ is the product of the differences $a_j-a_i$, and distinct nodes give exactly one interpolating polynomial.

formal.difference: The declaration states the determinant formula only. It does not state the invertibility criterion or the interpolation claim.

proofs.name: Induction on the number of nodes
proofs.slogan: Replace the last node by a variable, find its roots, and read the determinant as a product.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Repeated nodes make two rows equal, so both sides are $0$ and the formula still holds.

roles.why: Cofactor expansion and division by $X-a_i$ work over a field.
The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ start the induction.
Distinct nodes make $\det V$ nonzero, so the system $Vc=y$ has one solution.

steps.slogan: Check the cases $n=0$ and $n=1$.
steps.detail: For $n=0$ the determinant is $1$, which equals the empty product. For $n=1$ it is also $1$. Assume the formula for $n-1$ nodes.

steps.slogan: Replace the last node by a variable and expand along the last row.
steps.detail: This gives a polynomial $D(X)$ of degree at most $n-1$. Its leading coefficient is the [determinant](c:determinant) of the first $n-1$ nodes, because the last cofactor has sign $+$.

steps.slogan: Show that $D$ vanishes at each earlier node.
steps.detail: For $X=a_i$ with $i<n-1$, two rows of the matrix are equal. Swap them in each permutation term of the determinant and pair terms of opposite sign. So $D(a_i)=0$ for each earlier node, and the polynomial $D$ has these roots.

steps.slogan: Factor $D$ by its distinct roots and read off the product.
steps.detail: For distinct earlier nodes, each root gives a factor $X-a_i$, because $X^k-a^k$ is divisible by $X-a$. So $D(X)$ is its leading coefficient times $\prod_{i<n-1}(X-a_i)$. The induction hypothesis gives that coefficient. Set $X=a_{n-1}$. If earlier nodes repeat, two rows are equal and both sides are $0$.

steps.slogan: Solve the interpolation system with the adjugate of $V$.
steps.detail: If $\det V\ne0$, the inverse is $\operatorname{adj}(V)/\det V$, so $Vc=y$ has exactly one solution $c$. That $c$ is the coefficient vector of the [polynomial](c:polynomial). If $\det V=0$, the nodes repeat and the rows of $V$ are dependent.

concepts.c:field: Division by $X-a_i$ and cofactor expansion need a field.
concepts.c:vandermonde-determinant: The matrix with powers of the nodes is the object of the formula.
concepts.c:polynomial: The interpolating object is a polynomial of degree below $n$.
concepts.c:determinant: The product formula and the invertibility test both come from the determinant.

statement: A [primitive polynomial](c:primitive-polynomial) in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ has coprime coefficients. (1) A product of primitive polynomials is primitive. (2) A primitive $f$ is [irreducible](c:irreducible) in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ if and only if it is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$. (3) If $f$ is monic and irreducible modulo a prime $p$, then $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.

hypotheses.text: In (1) and (2), the polynomials are [primitive](c:primitive-polynomial) and nonzero.
In (3), the polynomial $f$ is monic with integer coefficients.
In (3), the reduction of $f$ modulo the prime $p$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$.

conclusion: Products of primitive polynomials are primitive, irreducibility over $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ agree for primitive polynomials, and a monic $f$ that is irreducible modulo $p$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states part (1) only, for polynomials over a general ring with a suitable gcd structure. Parts (2) and (3) are not in it.

proofs.name: Reduce modulo a prime
proofs.slogan: Show that a prime cannot divide a product of primitive polynomials, then clear denominators and reduce modulo $p$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in three parts. Part (3) uses part (2) and the degree-preserving reduction of a monic polynomial.

roles.why: Primitivity says that no prime divides all coefficients, which drives parts (1) and (2).
A monic polynomial is primitive, and its degree survives reduction modulo $p$.
Irreducibility of the reduction contradicts a proper factorization of $f$.

steps.slogan: Show that a product of primitive polynomials is primitive.
steps.detail: Suppose a prime $p$ divides every coefficient of $fg$. Reduce modulo $p$ in $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$, which is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain). Then $\bar f\bar g=0$, so $\bar f=0$ or $\bar g=0$. That contradicts primitivity of $f$ or $g$.

steps.slogan: Clear denominators to carry irreducibility from the integers to the rationals.
steps.detail: Let $f=GH$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ with both degrees positive. Write $G=(a/b)G_1$ and $H=(c/d)H_1$ with $G_1,H_1$ primitive. Then $f=rG_1H_1$ with $G_1H_1$ primitive by step 1. Since $f$ is also primitive, $r=\pm1$. So $f=\pm G_1H_1$ is a proper factorization in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

steps.slogan: Carry irreducibility from the rationals back to the integers.
steps.detail: Let $f=gh$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Over $\mathbb{Q}$ one factor, say $g=c$, is a nonzero constant. The integer $c$ divides every coefficient of $f$. Since $f$ is primitive, $c=\pm1$, so $g$ is a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

steps.slogan: Make the factors of a monic integer factorization monic.
steps.detail: Let $f=gh$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $g,h$ not units. The leading coefficients multiply to $1$, so they are equal and equal to $\pm1$. Replace $(g,h)$ by $(-g,-h)$ if needed. Both are then monic of degree at least $1$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the monic factorization modulo $p$ to contradict irreducibility.
steps.detail: The leading coefficient $1$ survives, so $\bar f=\bar g\bar h$ with $\deg\bar g=\deg g\ge1$ and $\deg\bar h=\deg h\ge1$. This is a proper factorization of $\bar f$, against the hypothesis. So $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and by step 2 in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three parts of the theorem.
steps.detail: Part (1) is step 1. Part (2) is steps 2 and 3. Part (3) is step 5.

concepts.c:primitive-polynomial: Primitivity is what stops a prime from dividing every coefficient.
concepts.c:irreducible: The theorem compares irreducibility over $\mathbb{Z}$ and over $\mathbb{Q}$.
concepts.c:integral-domain: The ring $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$ has no zero divisors, so a product is zero only if a factor is zero.

statement: Let $p$ be an odd prime and $p\nmid a$. Then $a^{(p-1)/2}\equiv\pm1\pmod p$, and $a$ is a [quadratic residue](c:quadratic-residue) if and only if the sign is $+1$. Exactly $(p-1)/2$ nonzero residues are squares. If $p\equiv3\pmod4$ and $a$ is a square, then $a^{(p+1)/4}$ is a square root of $a$.

hypotheses.text: The number $p$ is an odd [prime number](c:prime-number).
The integer $a$ is not divisible by $p$.
For the square root formula, $p\equiv3\pmod4$.

conclusion: The [Legendre symbol](c:legendre-symbol) $(a/p)$ equals $a^{(p-1)/2}$ modulo $p$, half of the nonzero residues are squares, and the explicit root formula holds.

formal.difference: The declaration states the criterion for squares in the field ZMod p. The count of squares and the root formula for $p\equiv3\pmod4$ are not in it.

proofs.name: Root counting in a finite field
proofs.slogan: Count squares by the two-to-one squaring map, then count roots of $X^{(p-1)/2}-1$ to identify them.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{Z}/p$. The remark that $-1$ is a square exactly when $p\equiv1\pmod4$ is the case $a=-1$.

roles.why: Oddness gives $x\ne-x$, and primality makes $\mathbb{Z}/p$ a field with no zero divisors.
A residue prime to $p$ is a unit, so Fermat's little theorem applies to it.
The exponent $(p+1)/4$ is an integer only when $p\equiv3\pmod4$.

steps.slogan: Show that squaring is exactly two to one on the nonzero residues.
steps.detail: In the field $F=\mathbb{Z}/p$, $x^2=y^2$ gives $(x-y)(x+y)=0$, so $y=\pm x$. Since $p$ is odd, $x\ne-x$ for $x\ne0$. So the set $S$ of nonzero squares has $(p-1)/2$ elements.

steps.slogan: Show that every nonzero square is a root of $X^{(p-1)/2}-1$.
steps.detail: A square $s=x^2$ has $s^{(p-1)/2}=x^{p-1}=1$ by Fermat's little theorem. So every nonzero square is a root of this polynomial.

steps.slogan: Count roots to identify the squares with the roots.
steps.detail: The polynomial $X^{(p-1)/2}-1$ has degree $(p-1)/2$, so at most $(p-1)/2$ roots in the [finite field](c:finite-field). It has the $(p-1)/2$ elements of $S$ as roots. So its roots are exactly $S$, and $a$ is a square if and only if $a^{(p-1)/2}=1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the power $a^{(p-1)/2}$ is $1$ or $-1$.
steps.detail: Put $b=a^{(p-1)/2}$. Then $b^2=a^{p-1}=1$ by Fermat's little theorem, so $(b-1)(b+1)=0$ and $b=\pm1$. By step 3, a non-square gives $b\ne1$, so $b=-1$.

steps.slogan: Build a square root of $a$ when $p\equiv3\pmod4$.
steps.detail: Then $(p+1)/4$ is an integer. For a square $a$, put $r=a^{(p+1)/4}$. So $r^2=a^{(p+1)/2}=a\cdot a^{(p-1)/2}=a$.

steps.slogan: Collect the four claims of the theorem.
steps.detail: The sign claim is step 4. The criterion and the count are steps 3 and 1. The root formula is step 5.

concepts.c:prime-number: Primality makes $\mathbb{Z}/p$ a field, which the root count needs.
concepts.c:quadratic-residue: The theorem decides which residues are squares.
concepts.c:legendre-symbol: The symbol records the sign of $a^{(p-1)/2}$.
concepts.c:finite-field: A nonzero polynomial over a field has at most as many roots as its degree.

statement: In a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the [nilpotent elements](c:nilpotent-element) are exactly the elements that lie in every [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal). More generally, the radical of an [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ is the intersection of the prime ideals that contain $I$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) with $1$.
For the general form, $I$ is an [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$.

conclusion: The set of nilpotent elements equals the intersection of all prime ideals, and $\sqrt I$ equals the intersection of the prime ideals that contain $I$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the nilradical form for a commutative ring. The general form for an ideal $I$ follows by passing to $R/I$.

proofs.name: Zorn's lemma on ideals that avoid the powers
proofs.slogan: Avoid the powers of a non-nilpotent element by a maximal ideal, and show that this ideal is prime.
proofs.scope: Both inclusions. The ring $R=0$ is allowed: it has no prime ideal and every element is nilpotent.

roles.why: Commutativity lets a maximal ideal that avoids the powers be shown prime.
The general form follows by applying the nilradical case to $R/I$.

steps.slogan: Show that a nilpotent element lies in every prime ideal.
steps.detail: If $x^n=0$ lies in a prime ideal $P$, then $x\in P$ by repeated use of primality.

steps.slogan: Fix a non-nilpotent $x$ and form the set of its powers.
steps.detail: Let $S=\{x,x^2,x^3,\dots\}$. Since $x$ is not nilpotent, no power of $x$ is zero, so $0\notin S$.

steps.slogan: Choose an ideal maximal among those that avoid the powers.
steps.detail: The set $\Sigma$ of ideals that do not meet $S$ contains $(0)$. A union of a chain in $\Sigma$ is again in $\Sigma$. By Zorn's lemma, $\Sigma$ has a maximal element $P$.

steps.slogan: Show that the maximal ideal $P$ is prime.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $x$ misses a prime ideal.
steps.detail: Since $x\in S$ and $P\cap S=\varnothing$, the element $x$ is not in $P$. So a non-nilpotent element is not in the intersection of all primes. With step 1, the nilradical equals that intersection.

concepts.c:nilpotent-element: Nilpotent elements are the elements that the theorem identifies.

statement: Every [doubly stochastic matrix](c:doubly-stochastic-matrix) is a convex combination of [permutation matrices](c:permutation-matrix). Conversely, every such combination is doubly stochastic. So the [extreme points](c:extreme-point) of the set of doubly stochastic matrices are exactly the permutation matrices.

hypotheses.text: The real $n\times n$ matrix $M$ has nonnegative entries.
Every row sum and every column sum of $M$ is $1$.
The size $n$ is at least $1$.

conclusion: The matrix $M=\sum_k\theta_kP_{\sigma_k}$ with $\theta_k>0$ and $\sum\theta_k=1$, and the extreme points are the permutation matrices.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the set of doubly stochastic matrices is the convex hull of the permutation matrices. The statement about extreme points is not in it.

proofs.name: Peel off one permutation matrix at a time
proofs.slogan: Find a permutation in the support by Hall's theorem, subtract it, and repeat on fewer positive entries.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The induction runs on the number of positive entries of $M$, which is at least $n$.

roles.why: Nonnegativity makes the support graph meaningful and keeps the peeled matrix nonnegative.
Equal row and column sums give Hall's condition and keep the peeled matrix doubly stochastic.
The permutation matrices are $n\times n$, and $n\ge1$ makes the support nonempty.

steps.slogan: Check that convex combinations of permutation matrices are doubly stochastic.
steps.detail: A permutation matrix has one entry $1$ in each row and column, and zeros elsewhere. A convex combination of nonnegative matrices with all line sums $1$ is nonnegative with all line sums $\sum\theta_k=1$.

steps.slogan: Find a permutation inside the support of $M$.
steps.detail: Join row $i$ to column $j$ when $M_{ij}>0$. For a set $R$ of rows with neighbor columns $N(R)$, $|R|=\sum_{i\in R,j\in N(R)}M_{ij}\le\sum_{j\in N(R)}\sum_iM_{ij}=|N(R)|$. By Hall's marriage theorem there is a perfect matching, that is, a permutation $\sigma$ with $M_{i,\sigma(i)}>0$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the smallest matched entry times the permutation matrix, then repeat.
steps.detail: Let $\theta=\min_iM_{i,\sigma(i)}$ and $P$ the matrix of $\sigma$. If $\theta=1$, then $M=P$. Otherwise $M'=(M-\theta P)/(1-\theta)$ is nonnegative with all line sums $1$, and it has fewer positive entries. By induction $M'$ is a convex combination, so $M=\theta P+(1-\theta)M'$ is one.

steps.slogan: Show that every permutation matrix is an extreme point.
steps.detail: Let $P=tA+(1-t)B$ with $0<t<1$ and $A,B$ doubly stochastic. Where $P$ is $0$, both $A$ and $B$ are $0$ by nonnegativity. Where $P$ is $1$, both entries are at most $1$ with weighted mean $1$, so both are $1$. So $A=B=P$.

steps.slogan: Show that every extreme point is a permutation matrix.
steps.detail: Write an extreme point $M=\sum_{k=1}^r\theta_kP_k$ with distinct $P_k$. If $r\ge2$, put $M'=\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{\theta_k}{1-\theta_1}P_k$, doubly stochastic by step 1. Then $M=\theta_1P_1+(1-\theta_1)M'$, so extremality forces $M'=P_1$ and $M=P_1$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three claims of the theorem.
steps.detail: The decomposition is step 3. The converse is step 1. The extreme points are steps 4 and 5.

concepts.c:doubly-stochastic-matrix: These matrices are the objects that the theorem decomposes.
concepts.c:permutation-matrix: Permutation matrices are the building blocks and the extreme points.
concepts.c:extreme-point: The theorem identifies the extreme points of the set.

statement: Let $u(n)$ be a [sequence](c:sequence) of reals with $u(m+n)\le u(m)+u(n)$ for all $m,n\ge1$. Then $u(n)/n$ has a [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) in $[-\infty,\infty)$, and this limit equals $\inf_{n\ge1}u(n)/n$. If $u(n)/n$ is bounded below, the limit is a real number.

hypotheses.text: The [sequence](c:sequence) satisfies $u(m+n)\le u(m)+u(n)$ for all positive integers $m$ and $n$.

conclusion: The [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) of $u(n)/n$ exists and equals $\inf_{n\ge1}u(n)/n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the inequality that the limit is at most each $u(n)/n$. The full statement that the limit equals the infimum is not in it.

proofs.name: Blocks of a fixed length
proofs.slogan: Cut each large index into blocks of a fixed length $n$, bound $u$ by the blocks, and let the index grow.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including the case of infimum $-\infty$. No growth bound on $u$ is needed.

roles.why: Subadditivity bounds $u(kn+r)$ by $k\,u(n)+u(r)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the limit inferior from below by the infimum.
steps.detail: Put $L=\inf_{n\ge1}u(n)/n\in[-\infty,\infty)$. By definition $u(N)/N\ge L$ for every $N$, so $\liminf u(N)/N\ge L$.

steps.slogan: Split an index into blocks of a fixed length $n$.
steps.detail: By induction on $k$, $u(kn+r)\le k\,u(n)+u(r)$. Indeed $u((k+1)n+r)\le u(n)+u(kn+r)$. Write $N=kn+r$ with $1\le r\le n$ and let $M_n=\max_{r\le n}u(r)$. Then $u(N)\le k\,u(n)+M_n$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $N$ and let $N$ grow with $n$ fixed.
steps.detail: We get $u(N)/N\le(kn/N)(u(n)/n)+M_n/N$. As $N\to\infty$, $kn/N\to1$ and $M_n/N\to0$. So $\limsup u(N)/N\le u(n)/n$ for every $n$.

steps.slogan: Take the infimum over $n$ to squeeze the limit.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $\limsup u(N)/N\le L$. With step 1, $\limsup\le L\le\liminf$. So the limit exists and equals $L$. If $L=-\infty$, then $u(N)/N\to-\infty$. If $u(n)/n$ is bounded below, $L$ is real.

concepts.c:sequence: The theorem concerns the sequence $u(n)/n$ built from a subadditive $u$.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The proof squeezes the limit between the limit inferior and the limit superior.

statement: Let $f\colon[a,b]\times E\to E$ be [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) in the second variable with constant $K$. If $x$ and $y$ solve the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $z'=f(t,z)$ on $[a,b]$, then $\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le\|x(a)-y(a)\|e^{K(t-a)}$. So a solution of the [initial value problem](c:initial-value-problem) is unique.

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ is [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) in the second variable, with a constant $K\ge0$ that does not depend on $t$.
The functions $x,y\colon[a,b]\to E$ are continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and solve the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $z'=f(t,z)$ there.

conclusion: For every $t\in[a,b]$, $\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le\|x(a)-y(a)\|e^{K(t-a)}$, and equal initial values give equal solutions.

formal.difference: The declaration states a comparison bound for trajectories of a Lipschitz field, in a related form. The exponential bound for continuous dependence and the uniqueness claim are stated here.

proofs.name: Barrier and mean value inequality
proofs.slogan: Trap the norm of the difference below an exponential barrier by a last-time argument.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem on $[a,b]$. The Lipschitz bound is used only at the points $x(t)$ and $y(t)$.

roles.why: The Lipschitz bound turns $\|v'\|$ into at most $K\|v\|$.
The equations give the derivative of the difference $v=x-y$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two solutions and bound the derivative of the difference.
steps.detail: Put $v=x-y$ and $\delta=\|v(a)\|$. Then $v'(t)=f(t,x(t))-f(t,y(t))$, and the [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) bound gives $\|v'(t)\|\le K\|v(t)\|$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\|v\|$ with a slightly larger exponential barrier.
steps.detail: Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and put $B(t)=(\delta+\varepsilon)e^{K(t-a)}$. Then $B'=KB$ and $\|v(a)\|<B(a)$. Let $T$ be the supremum of the times $\tau$ with $\|v\|\le B$ on $[a,\tau]$. By continuity $\|v\|\le B$ on $[a,T]$.

steps.slogan: Bound the growth of $v$ on $[a,T]$ by the mean value inequality.
steps.detail: On $(a,T)$, $\|v'\|\le K\|v\|\le KB=B'$. The mean value inequality with boundary function $B$ gives $\|v(t)-v(a)\|\le B(t)-B(a)$. So $\|v(t)\|\le B(t)-\varepsilon$ for $t\in(a,T]$, and $\|v(T)\|<B(T)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $T=b$ by continuity.
steps.detail: If $T<b$, continuity and $\|v(T)\|<B(T)$ give $\|v\|<B$ on $[T,T+\eta)$ for some $\eta>0$. This contradicts the choice of $T$. So $\|v(t)\|\le(\delta+\varepsilon)e^{K(t-a)}$ on $[a,b]$.

steps.slogan: Let $arepsilon$ tend to $0$ and read the uniqueness.
steps.detail: The bound holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $\|v(t)\|\le\delta e^{K(t-a)}$. If $x(a)=y(a)$, then $\delta=0$ and $x=y$ on $[a,b]$. This is uniqueness for the [initial value problem](c:initial-value-problem).

concepts.c:lipschitz-function: The Lipschitz bound controls the derivative of the difference by its size.
concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: Both functions solve the same equation, so their difference has a controlled derivative.
concepts.c:initial-value-problem: Uniqueness for the initial value problem follows from the bound.

statement: For every complex $z\notin\mathbb{Z}$, $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin(\pi z)$, where $\Gamma$ is the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function). Hence $\Gamma$ has no zeros, $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, and $|\Gamma(1/2+it)|^2=\pi/\cosh(\pi t)$ for real $t$.

hypotheses.text: The number $z$ is complex and not an integer.

conclusion: The product $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)$ equals $\pi/\sin(\pi z)$, the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function) has no zeros, $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$, and $|\Gamma(1/2+it)|^2=\pi/\cosh(\pi t)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the reflection formula. The statements on zeros, on $\Gamma(1/2)$ and on the modulus on the critical line are consequences proved here.

proofs.name: Gauss products and the sine product
proofs.slogan: Multiply the Gauss products for $z$ and $1-z$ into an exact identity, then pass to the limit with the sine product.
proofs.scope: All complex $z\notin\mathbb{Z}$. At integers one factor is at a pole and $\sin(\pi z)=0$.

roles.why: For $z\notin\mathbb{Z}$, neither $z$ nor $1-z$ is a pole and every denominator is nonzero.

steps.slogan: Write both Gamma values as limits of Gauss products.
steps.detail: The Gauss limit formula gives $G_n(z)\to\Gamma(z)$ and $G_n(1-z)\to\Gamma(1-z)$. So the product $G_n(z)G_n(1-z)$ tends to $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)$ as $n$ grows.

steps.slogan: Multiply the two Gauss products into an exact finite identity.
steps.detail: The factors $n^z$ and $n^{1-z}$ multiply to $n$. Pulling out the last factor $n+1-z$ leaves $\prod_{j\le n}(j^2-z^2)=(n!)^2\prod_{j\le n}(1-z^2/j^2)$. So $G_n(z)G_n(1-z)=n\big/\big((n+1-z)\,z\prod_{j\le n}(1-z^2/j^2)\big)$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit with the Euler sine product.
steps.detail: We have $n/(n+1-z)\to1$, and the partial [infinite product](c:infinite-product) tends to $\sin(\pi z)/(\pi z)\ne0$. So the right side tends to $\pi/\sin(\pi z)$. With step 1, $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin(\pi z)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Gamma function has no zeros.
steps.detail: For $z\notin\mathbb{Z}$, the product $\pi/\sin(\pi z)$ is finite and nonzero, so $\Gamma(z)\ne0$. At positive integers $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!>0$. At $0,-1,-2,\dots$ the function $\Gamma$ has a simple pole, so it takes no value there.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $\Gamma(1/2)$ and the modulus on the critical line.
steps.detail: At $z=1/2$, $\Gamma(1/2)^2=\pi$, and $\Gamma(1/2)>0$ gives $\sqrt\pi$. For $z=1/2+it$, $1-z=\bar z$ and $\Gamma(\bar z)=\overline{\Gamma(z)}$, so $|\Gamma(z)|^2=\pi/\sin(\pi/2+i\pi t)=\pi/\cosh(\pi t)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the claims of the theorem.
steps.detail: The reflection formula is step 3. The absence of zeros is step 4. The special values are step 5.

concepts.c:gamma-function: The theorem is about the product $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)$.
concepts.c:infinite-product: The sine function is the limit of a product that the proof uses.

statement: Let $C$ be a locally small [category](c:category) and $F\colon C^{op}\to\mathrm{Set}$ a [functor](c:functor). Then $\eta\mapsto\eta_X(\mathrm{id}_X)$ is a bijection from $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,X),F)$ to $F(X)$, natural in $X$ and $F$. So $X\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)$ is fully faithful, and $\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)\cong\mathrm{Hom}(-,Y)$ if and only if $X\cong Y$.

hypotheses.text: The [category](c:category) $C$ is locally small, so each $\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$ is a set.
The map $F$ is a [functor](c:functor) from $C^{op}$ to sets.

conclusion: The evaluation at $\mathrm{id}_X$ is a natural bijection, the Yoneda embedding is fully faithful, and [representable functors](c:representable-functor) determine their objects up to isomorphism.

formal.difference: The declaration states the bijection for the contravariant functor in the same form. The naturality, the full faithfulness and the isomorphism criterion are stated here.

proofs.name: Evaluate at the identity
proofs.slogan: Evaluate a natural transformation at the identity, invert by acting with $F$, and read the consequences.
proofs.scope: The contravariant form. The covariant form follows by applying the result to $C^{op}$.

roles.why: Local smallness makes $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(-,X),F)$ a set.
The functor $F$ supplies the maps $F(f)$ that define the inverse.

steps.slogan: Define the inverse map and show that it is inverse to evaluation.
steps.detail: For $x\in F(X)$ put $\Psi(x)_Y(f)=F(f)(x)$. It is natural because $F(f\circ g)=F(g)\circ F(f)$. Then $\Phi(\Psi(x))=F(\mathrm{id}_X)(x)=x$. For natural $\eta$, the naturality square for $f\colon Y\to X$ at $h=\mathrm{id}_X$ gives $\eta_Y(f)=F(f)(\eta_X(\mathrm{id}_X))$.

steps.slogan: Check that the bijection is natural in $F$ and in $X$.
steps.detail: For $\theta\colon F\to G$, $\Phi(\theta\circ\eta)=\theta_X(\Phi(\eta))$. For $h\colon X'\to X$, the naturality square of $\eta$ gives $\Phi(\eta\circ y(h))=F(h)(\Phi(\eta))$, where $y(X)=\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)$.

steps.slogan: Take $F=\mathrm{Hom}(-,Y)$ to get full faithfulness.
steps.detail: Then $\Phi\colon\mathrm{Nat}(y(X),y(Y))\to\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)$ is a bijection with $\Phi(y(g))=g$. So $g\mapsto y(g)$ is a bijection onto $\mathrm{Nat}(y(X),y(Y))$, and the embedding $y$ is fully faithful.

steps.slogan: Reflect isomorphisms along the fully faithful embedding.
steps.detail: A functor keeps isomorphisms, so $X\cong Y$ gives $y(X)\cong y(Y)$. Conversely an isomorphism $\eta=y(g)$ with inverse $y(h)$ gives $y(h\circ g)=y(\mathrm{id}_X)$. Faithfulness gives $h\circ g=\mathrm{id}_X$, and likewise $g\circ h=\mathrm{id}_Y$.

steps.slogan: Collect the claims of the theorem.
steps.detail: The bijection is step 1 and its naturality is step 2. Full faithfulness is step 3 and the isomorphism criterion is step 4.

concepts.c:category: The theorem holds for every locally small category.
concepts.c:functor: The functor $F$ and the embedding $y$ are the two functors compared.
concepts.c:representable-functor: The functor $\mathrm{Hom}(-,X)$ is the representable functor that the lemma studies.

statement: Let $p_0,\dots,p_n$ be [affinely independent](c:affine-independence) points of a real [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space). Exactly one point $c$ of their affine span is equally distant from all $p_i$. This is the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter). With $v_j=p_j-p_0$, we have $c=p_0+\sum\lambda_jv_j$ where $G\lambda=b$, $G_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle$ and $b_i=|v_i|^2/2$.

hypotheses.text: The ambient space is a real [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
The points $p_0,\dots,p_n$ are [affinely independent](c:affine-independence), that is, $v_1,\dots,v_n$ are linearly independent.

conclusion: There is exactly one equidistant point $c$ in the affine span, the matrix $G$ is invertible, and every equidistant point of the whole space is $c$ plus a vector orthogonal to the span.

formal.difference: The declaration states existence and uniqueness of the circumcenter in the span. The Gram system and the description of equidistant points outside the span are stated here.

proofs.name: Linear system with the Gram matrix
proofs.slogan: Turn equal distances into a linear system with a Gram matrix, and solve it because the Gram matrix is invertible.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The point $c$ must lie in the affine span, or it is not unique when $n$ is below the dimension.

roles.why: The inner product gives the squared distances and the Gram matrix.
Independence of the $v_j$ makes the kernel of $G$ trivial.

steps.slogan: Turn equal distance into linear equations in the coordinates.
steps.detail: Write $c=p_0+u$ with $u=\sum\lambda_jv_j$. The condition $|c-p_i|=|c-p_0|$ becomes $|u-v_i|^2=|u|^2$, that is $\langle u,v_i\rangle=|v_i|^2/2$. So the conditions for $i=1,\dots,n$ read $G\lambda=b$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Gram matrix is invertible.
steps.detail: If $Gx=0$, then $x^TGx=|\sum x_jv_j|^2=0$, so $\sum x_jv_j=0$. By [linear independence](c:linear-independence), $x=0$. So $G$ has trivial kernel.

steps.slogan: Solve the system to get exactly one circumcenter.
steps.detail: Since $G$ is invertible, $G\lambda=b$ has exactly one solution. So exactly one $c$ in the affine span has equal distance to all $p_i$. The common distance $r=|u|$ is the circumradius of the [circumcenter](c:circumcenter).

steps.slogan: Project an equidistant point of the whole space onto the span.
steps.detail: Let $q$ be equidistant from all $p_i$ and let $c'$ be its orthogonal projection on the affine span. By Pythagoras, $|q-p_i|^2=|q-c'|^2+|c'-p_i|^2$, so $c'$ is also equidistant. By step 3, $c'=c$. So $q=c+w$ with $w$ orthogonal to the span.

concepts.c:euclidean-space: The inner product defines distances and the Gram matrix.
concepts.c:affine-independence: Affine independence makes the vectors $v_j$ independent, so $G$ is invertible.
concepts.c:linear-independence: Independence of the $v_j$ gives the trivial kernel of $G$.
concepts.c:circumcenter: The theorem proves that the circumcenter exists and is unique.

statement: The [boundary](c:boundary) of a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ has [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) zero. So $C$ is Lebesgue measurable. If $C$ is bounded, the cubes of the lattice $h\mathbb{Z}^d$ that meet $C$ but are not inside it have total volume at most $\varepsilon(h)$, where $\varepsilon(h)\to0$ as $h\to0$.

hypotheses.text: The set $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ is [convex](c:convex-set). It need not be open, closed or bounded.
For the grid claim only, $C$ is bounded.

conclusion: The boundary of $C$ has measure zero, $C$ is measurable, and the outer and inner grid approximations of the volume differ by at most $\varepsilon(h)\to0$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the frontier of a convex set has zero Haar measure. The measurability and the grid statement are stated here.

proofs.name: Shrink the closure into the interior
proofs.slogan: Show that a shrunken copy of the closure lies in the interior, so the boundary lies in a thin shell.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A convex set with empty interior lies in a hyperplane, which is a separate easy case.

roles.why: Convexity makes $tk+(1-t)B_{r/2}$ lie in $C$, which puts $tK$ in the interior.
Boundedness gives a finite measure for the closure and for the neighborhoods of the boundary.

steps.slogan: Treat the case of empty interior.
steps.detail: If the affine hull of $C$ is a proper subspace, it lies in a hyperplane. Then the closure lies in the same hyperplane, which has measure $0$. So the [boundary](c:boundary) has measure $0$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a bounded set that contains a ball.
steps.detail: Otherwise translate an interior point to $0$ and pick $B_r\subset C$. The sets $C_n=C\cap B(0,n)$ are convex, bounded and contain $B_r$, and $\partial C\subset\bigcup_n\partial C_n$. A countable union of null sets is null.

steps.slogan: Show that the shrunken closure lies in the interior.
steps.detail: Let $K=\overline C$ and $0<t<1$. For $k\in K$ pick $c\in C$ close to $k$. Then $tk+(1-t)b=tc+(1-t)b'$ with $b'\in B_r\subset C$, for all small $b$. So $tk+(1-t)B_{r/2}\subset C$, and $tK\subset\operatorname{int}C$.

steps.slogan: Bound the boundary by a thin shell and measure the shell.
steps.detail: By step 3, $\partial C\subset K\setminus tK$. The map $x\mapsto tx$ scales [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) by $t^d$, so the shell has measure $(1-t^d)\operatorname{Leb}(K)$. Let $t\to1$ to get $\operatorname{Leb}(\partial C)=0$. Then $C=\operatorname{int}C\cup(C\cap\partial C)$ is measurable.

steps.slogan: Cover the boundary cubes by a neighborhood of the boundary.
steps.detail: A cube $Q$ of $h\mathbb{Z}^d$ that meets $C$ and its complement meets $\partial C$, by [connectedness](c:connected-space) of a segment in $Q$. So $Q$ lies in $N(\sqrt d\,h)=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial C)\le\sqrt d\,h\}$. These closed bounded sets decrease to $\partial C$ with measure $0$, so $\varepsilon(h)=\operatorname{Leb}N(\sqrt d\,h)\to0$.

concepts.c:boundary: The theorem says that the boundary of a convex set is null.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity is the property that puts the shrunken closure inside the set.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Scaling changes Lebesgue measure by a power of the factor.
concepts.c:connected-space: A segment is connected, so it meets the boundary if it meets both sides.

statement: Let $K$ be a nonempty closed [convex set](c:convex-set) in a real [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space). A point $v\in K$ is nearest to $u$ iff $\langle u-v,w-v\rangle\le0$ for all $w\in K$. This point $P_Ku$ exists, is unique and is 1-Lipschitz in $u$. For convex differentiable $f$, $v$ minimizes $f$ on $K$ iff $v=P_K(v-\eta\nabla f(v))$ for any $\eta>0$.

hypotheses.text: The set $K$ is a nonempty closed [convex set](c:convex-set) in a real Hilbert space.
In part (c) the function $f$ is [convex](c:convex-function) and differentiable.
The step size $\eta>0$ is arbitrary, and the [gradient](c:gradient) test does not depend on it.

conclusion: The nearest point $P_Ku$ exists, is unique, is characterized by the variational inequality, is nonexpansive, and gives the fixed-point test for minimizers.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the equivalence of the nearest-point property and the variational inequality. Existence, nonexpansiveness and the fixed-point test are stated here.

proofs.name: Perturb along a segment
proofs.slogan: Move along segments inside the set, read off the variational inequality, then derive each consequence.
proofs.scope: The full statement (a), (b), (c). The Hilbert projection theorem supplies existence.

roles.why: Convexity keeps the segment from $v$ to $w$ inside $K$, and closedness gives existence.
Convexity of $f$ gives the sufficiency of the first-order condition.
The factor $\eta$ only scales the inner product, so it does not change the sign test.

steps.slogan: Test a nearest point along segments to get the inequality.
steps.detail: Let $v$ be nearest and $w\in K$. For $\theta\in(0,1]$, $v+\theta(w-v)\in K$. So $\|u-v\|^2\le\|u-v\|^2-2\theta\langle u-v,w-v\rangle+\theta^2\|w-v\|^2$. Divide by $\theta$ and let $\theta\to0$. Conversely, if the inequality holds, $\|u-w\|^2\ge\|u-v\|^2+\|w-v\|^2$, so $v$ is nearest and unique.

steps.slogan: Get a nearest point from the projection theorem.
steps.detail: A nonempty closed convex set in a Hilbert space has a nearest point to $u$. With step 1 it is unique. Call it $P_Ku$.

steps.slogan: Add the two inequalities for $u$ and $u'$ to show nonexpansiveness.
steps.detail: Put $p=P_Ku$ and $p'=P_Ku'$. The inequalities $\langle u-p,p'-p\rangle\le0$ and $\langle u'-p',p-p'\rangle\le0$ add up to $\|p-p'\|^2\le\langle u-u',p-p'\rangle$. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality then gives $\|p-p'\|\le\|u-u'\|$.

steps.slogan: Show that the first-order condition characterizes minimizers.
steps.detail: If $v$ minimizes $f$ on $K$, then $g(\theta)=f(v+\theta(w-v))$ has its minimum at $0$, so $g'(0)=\langle\nabla f(v),w-v\rangle\ge0$. Conversely, convexity gives $f(w)\ge f(v)+\langle\nabla f(v),w-v\rangle\ge f(v)$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the first-order condition as a projection fixed-point test.
steps.detail: Put $u=v-\eta\nabla f(v)$. Then $\langle u-v,w-v\rangle=-\eta\langle\nabla f(v),w-v\rangle$. This is at most $0$ for all $w\in K$ exactly when the first-order condition holds. By step 1, that is exactly $v=P_Ku$.

steps.slogan: Collect the parts (a), (b) and (c).
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give part (a). Step 3 gives part (b). Steps 4 and 5 give part (c).

concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity keeps segments from the nearest point inside the set.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The inner product and completeness give the inequality and the nearest point.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of $f$ gives the converse of the first-order condition.
concepts.c:gradient: The gradient of $f$ defines the projection fixed-point test.

statement: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field) and $A,B$ be $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) over $k$. Then $A,B$ are similar iff $xI-A$ and $xI-B$ have the same invariant factors $d_1\mid\dots\mid d_n$ of the [Smith normal form](c:smith-normal-form). The product of the $d_i$ is the [characteristic polynomial](c:characteristic-polynomial), $d_n$ is the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial), and $A$ is similar to the block matrix of companion matrices.

hypotheses.text: The ring $k[x]$ over the [field](c:field) $k$ is a Euclidean domain, so Smith normal form exists.
The [matrices](c:matrix) $A$ and $B$ are square of the same size $n$.
Similar means $B=PAP^{-1}$ for an invertible $P$ over $k$.

conclusion: Similarity of $A$ and $B$ is equivalent to equality of their invariant factors, which give the characteristic polynomial, the minimal polynomial and the rational canonical form.

formal.difference: The declaration relates the characteristic matrix to a polynomial matrix. The classification by invariant factors is not in it.

proofs.name: Turn a matrix into a module
proofs.slogan: Turn $A$ into a $k[x]$-module, present it by $xI-A$, and read all data from Smith normal form.
proofs.scope: The full statement over any field. The Smith normal form theorem over $k[x]$ is cited.

roles.why: The Euclidean property of $k[x]$ gives Smith normal form of $xI-A$.
Both matrices act on $k^n$, so both give modules of the same rank.
Similarity is the same as an isomorphism of the modules $V_A$ and $V_B$.

steps.slogan: Make $k^n$ a $k[x]$-module and present it by $xI-A$.
steps.detail: Let $x$ act on $V_A=k^n$ as $A$. Then $A,B$ are similar iff $V_A\cong V_B$. The map $\varphi\colon k[x]^n\to V_A$, $\sum x^mv_m\mapsto\sum A^mv_m$, is $k[x]$-linear and onto. Its kernel is the image of $xI-A$, and $xI-A$ is injective because its determinant is nonzero. So $V_A\cong\operatorname{coker}(xI-A)$.

steps.slogan: Show that similarity equals equivalence of the characteristic matrices.
steps.detail: If $B=PAP^{-1}$, then $P(xI-A)P^{-1}=xI-B$, and $P$ is invertible over $k[x]$. Conversely, if $U(xI-A)V=xI-B$ with $U,V$ invertible, then $U$ induces an isomorphism of the cokernels. By step 1, $V_A\cong V_B$, so $A,B$ are similar.

steps.slogan: Compare the Smith normal forms.
steps.detail: Matrices over $k[x]$ are equivalent iff they have the same Smith normal form. So $A,B$ are similar iff their monic invariant factors agree.

steps.slogan: Read the characteristic and minimal polynomials from the invariant factors.
steps.detail: The last determinantal divisor of $xI-A$ is $\det(xI-A)=\chi_A$, and it equals $d_1\cdots d_n$. Also $V_A\cong\bigoplus k[x]/(d_i)$, and $d_n$ kills every summand, but no proper divisor of $d_n$ kills $k[x]/(d_n)$. So the annihilator of $V_A$ is $(d_n)$, and $d_n$ is the minimal polynomial.

steps.slogan: Choose a basis of each summand to get the block form.
steps.detail: For monic $d$ of degree $m$, the classes of $1,x,\dots,x^{m-1}$ form a $k$-basis of $k[x]/(d)$, and $x$ acts as the companion matrix $C(d)$. Joining these bases gives a basis in which $A$ is $\operatorname{diag}(C(d_i))$. By step 3 this block form depends only on the similarity class.

steps.slogan: Collect the claims of the theorem.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give the similarity criteria. Step 4 gives the characteristic and minimal polynomials. Step 5 gives the rational canonical form.

concepts.c:field: The ground field makes $k[x]$ a Euclidean domain.
concepts.c:matrix: The matrices $A$ and $B$ define the modules and their presentations.
concepts.c:similarity-transformation: Similarity is what the module isomorphism encodes.
concepts.c:smith-normal-form: Smith normal form of $xI-A$ gives the invariant factors.
concepts.c:characteristic-polynomial: It equals the product of the invariant factors.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: It equals the last invariant factor.

statement: Let $\zeta$ be a [primitive root of unity](c:is-primitive-root) of order $n\ge1$. Then $\Phi_n$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$, so $[\mathbb Q(\zeta):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(n)$. The extension is a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension), and $a\mapsto\sigma_a$ with $\sigma_a(\zeta)=\zeta^a$ is a group isomorphism $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times\to\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\zeta)/\mathbb Q)$. In particular the extension is abelian.

hypotheses.text: The order $n$ is a positive integer, and $\varphi$ is the [Euler totient function](c:euler-s-totient-function).
The number $\zeta\in\mathbb C$ is a [primitive root of unity](c:is-primitive-root) of order $n$.

conclusion: The cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_n$ is irreducible, and the Galois group of $\mathbb Q(\zeta)/\mathbb Q$ is isomorphic to $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the isomorphism of the Galois group with the units, for a cyclotomic extension in which $\Phi_n$ is known to be irreducible. The irreducibility proof is given here.

proofs.name: Frobenius and a squarefree reduction
proofs.slogan: Show that the minimal polynomial of $\zeta$ is stable under $p$-th powers, then count automorphisms.
proofs.scope: The full statement for every $n\ge1$. Gauss lemma and the factorization of $x^n-1$ are cited.

roles.why: The assumption $p\nmid n$ makes $x^n-1$ squarefree modulo $p$, and $\varphi(n)$ counts the primitive roots.
The primitive root generates the field and every power coprime to $n$ is again primitive.

steps.slogan: Show that the minimal polynomial of $\zeta$ divides $\Phi_n$ and has integer coefficients.
steps.detail: $\Phi_n$ is monic in $\mathbb Z[x]$, has degree $\varphi(n)$, and its roots are the primitive $n$-th roots of unity. Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $\zeta$. Then $f\mid\Phi_n$. By Gauss lemma, $f$ equals a monic irreducible factor of $\Phi_n$ in $\mathbb Z[x]$, so $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$.

steps.slogan: Reduce modulo a prime to compare $f$ with the minimal polynomial of $\eta^p$.
steps.detail: Let $\eta$ be a root of $f$, let $p\nmid n$ be prime, and let $g$ be the minimal polynomial of $\eta^p$. Suppose $g\ne f$. Then $g(x^p)=f\,k$ in $\mathbb Z[x]$, and $f g\mid x^n-1$. Modulo $p$, the [Frobenius](c:frobenius) identity gives $\bar g^p=\bar g(x^p)=\bar f\bar k$. So an irreducible factor $\pi$ of $\bar f$ divides $\bar g$, and $\pi^2\mid x^n-1$ in $\mathbb F_p[x]$.

steps.slogan: Contradict this with squarefreeness of $x^n-1$ modulo $p$.
steps.detail: The derivative of $x^n-1$ is $nx^{n-1}$, and $n\ne0$ in $\mathbb F_p$. The derivative has only the root $0$, which is not a root of $x^n-1$. So $x^n-1$ is squarefree in $\mathbb F_p[x]$. This contradicts the first claim. Hence $g=f$.

steps.slogan: Move from $\zeta$ to every primitive root and conclude irreducibility.
steps.detail: Every primitive root is $\zeta^k$ with $\gcd(k,n)=1$. Write $k=p_1\cdots p_r$ with primes $p_i\nmid n$. Apply step 3 $r$ times to get that $\zeta^k$ is a root of $f$. So $f$ has all $\varphi(n)$ primitive roots as roots, $\Phi_n\mid f$, and $f=\Phi_n$. Thus $[\mathbb Q(\zeta):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(n)$.

steps.slogan: Count the automorphisms and build the isomorphism.
steps.detail: $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$ is the splitting field of $x^n-1$, so the extension is Galois of degree $\varphi(n)$. Each automorphism $\sigma$ sends $\zeta$ to a root $\zeta^a$ of $\Phi_n$ with $a\in(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$, and is determined by $a$. Since $\sigma_a\sigma_b(\zeta)=\zeta^{ab}$, the map $a\mapsto\sigma_a$ is an injective homomorphism between groups of order $\varphi(n)$. So it is an isomorphism.

concepts.c:euler-s-totient-function: It gives the degree of $\Phi_n$ and the order of the Galois group.
concepts.c:is-primitive-root: The primitive root generates the field and its powers coprime to $n$ are the roots of $\Phi_n$.
concepts.c:galois-extension: The extension is Galois because the field splits $x^n-1$.
concepts.c:frobenius: The $p$-th power map in characteristic $p$ turns $g(x^p)$ into $g^p$.

statement: Take a regular [Sturm-Liouville problem](c:sturm-liouville-problem) $-(py')'+qy=\lambda wy$ on $[a,b]$ with $p,w>0$ and real separated boundary conditions. Then every eigenvalue is real. [Eigenfunctions](c:eigenvector) for different eigenvalues are [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) for the weight $w$. Each eigenspace has dimension $1$.

hypotheses.text: The problem is regular: $p,q,w$ are continuous, real, and $p,w>0$ on the closed interval.
The boundary conditions are separated and real, each with a nonzero coefficient pair.
The theorem does not claim that an [eigenfunction](c:eigenvector) exists.

conclusion: Eigenvalues are real, eigenfunctions of different eigenvalues are orthogonal with weight $w$, and each eigenspace is one dimensional.

formal.difference: The declaration states that eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator on an inner product space are real. The orthogonality and simplicity parts, and the boundary-value setting, are stated here.

proofs.name: Lagrange identity and the Wronskian
proofs.slogan: Show that the operator is symmetric on the boundary conditions, then read all three claims.
proofs.scope: Real and complex valued $C^2$ eigenfunctions on a regular interval. Existence of eigenvalues is not claimed.

roles.why: Real coefficients and positive $w$ make the Lagrange identity and positive integrals work.
The real separated conditions kill the boundary terms and give a one-dimensional kernel at $a$.
The proof does not need existence, so it only treats given eigenfunctions.

steps.slogan: Derive the Lagrange identity for the operator.
steps.detail: Put $B(u,v)=p(u\bar v'-u'\bar v)$. A direct derivative gives $B'=u(p\bar v')'-(pu')'\bar v$. Since $p,q$ are real, $\int_a^b[(Lu)\bar v-u\,\overline{Lv}]\,dx=B(u,v)(b)-B(u,v)(a)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the boundary terms vanish.
steps.detail: At $a$, the vectors $(u(a),p(a)u'(a))$ and $(\bar v(a),p(a)\bar v'(a))$ are killed by one nonzero real functional. So both lie in a one-dimensional kernel, and their determinant $B(u,v)(a)$ is $0$. The same holds at $b$. Hence $\int(Lu)\bar v=\int u\,\overline{Lv}$.

steps.slogan: Prove reality of eigenvalues.
steps.detail: Put $u=v=y$ with $Ly=\lambda wy$. Then $(\lambda-\bar\lambda)\int_a^bw|y|^2dx=0$. The integral is positive because $y\ne0$ is continuous and $w>0$. So $\lambda=\bar\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Prove orthogonality for different eigenvalues.
steps.detail: Let $Ly=\lambda wy$ and $Lz=\mu wz$ with $\lambda\ne\mu$ real. Step 2 gives $(\lambda-\mu)\int wy\bar z=0$. So $\int_a^bwy\bar z\,dx=0$.

steps.slogan: Prove that each eigenspace has dimension one.
steps.detail: Let $y,z$ have the same eigenvalue. Their initial vectors at $a$ lie in the same one-dimensional kernel, so $u=c_1y+c_2z$ with $(c_1,c_2)\ne0$ has $u(a)=pu'(a)=0$. It solves a linear first-order system with continuous coefficients, so uniqueness for the initial value problem gives $u\equiv0$. Hence $y,z$ are dependent.

statement: Let $f\colon[0,1]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) in the second variable with constant $L<8$. Then $y''=f(x,y)$, $y(0)=y(1)=0$ has exactly one $C^2$ solution. The iteration $y_{k+1}=Ty_k$ with the Green kernel converges to it uniformly, with $\|y_k-y\|_\infty\le(L/8)^k(1-L/8)^{-1}\|y_1-y_0\|_\infty$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is continuous and [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) in $u$ with a global constant $L<8$.
The problem is the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $y''=f(x,y)$ with Dirichlet conditions on $[0,1]$.
The starting function $y_0$ is any continuous function.

conclusion: The boundary value problem has a unique solution, and the Green function iteration converges to it with the stated geometric bound.

formal.difference: The declaration states the a priori bound for iterates of a contraction. The Green function reduction and the contraction constant $L/8$ are stated here.

proofs.name: Green function and contraction
proofs.slogan: Rewrite the problem as a fixed-point equation and show that the integral operator contracts for $L<8$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement on $[0,1]$ with Dirichlet conditions. The Banach fixed-point theorem is cited.

roles.why: The Lipschitz constant gives the contraction factor $L/8$ of $T$.
The equation and conditions are solved by the linear Green formula, which gives the integral form.
Any continuous start converges, because the fixed-point theorem allows any initial point.

steps.slogan: Solve the linear problem with the Green function.
steps.detail: For continuous $g$, put $u(x)=-(1-x)\int_0^xt\,g(t)dt-x\int_x^1(1-t)g(t)dt$. Two derivatives give $u''=g$, and $u(0)=u(1)=0$. If $u_1,u_2$ both solve it, $u_1-u_2$ is affine with two zeros, so it is $0$. Hence $u=-\int G\,g$.

steps.slogan: Show that solutions of the problem are the fixed points of $T$.
steps.detail: If $y\in C^2$ solves the problem, then $g=f(\cdot,y)$ is continuous and $y=-\int G\,g=Ty$. If $y=Ty$ with $y$ continuous, then step 1 shows $y\in C^2$ and $y''=f(\cdot,y)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the size of the kernel integral.
steps.detail: For $x\in[0,1]$, $\int_0^1|G(x,t)|dt$ splits at $t=x$ into $(1-x)x^2/2$ and $x(1-x)^2/2$. The sum is $x(1-x)/2$. This is at most $1/8$ for every $x$, with equality at $x=1/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $T$ is a contraction in the sup norm.
steps.detail: $T$ maps $C[0,1]$ to itself. For $y,z$, $|(Ty-Tz)(x)|\le\int|G(x,t)|L|y(t)-z(t)|dt\le(L/8)\|y-z\|_\infty$. So $T$ is a [contraction](c:contraction-mapping) with $q=L/8<1$.

steps.slogan: Apply the fixed-point theorem in the complete space $C[0,1]$.
steps.detail: $C[0,1]$ with the sup norm is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), so $T$ has one fixed point $y$ and $y_k\to y$ for every $y_0$. By step 2, $y$ is the unique $C^2$ solution. The standard estimate gives $\|y_k-y\|\le q^k(1-q)^{-1}\|y_1-y_0\|$.

concepts.c:lipschitz-function: The Lipschitz bound on $f$ makes $T$ a contraction.
concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: The problem is a boundary value problem for a second-order equation.
concepts.c:fixed-point: Solutions of the problem are fixed points of $T$.
concepts.c:contraction-mapping: A contraction has a unique fixed point and geometric iteration error.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of $C[0,1]$ is needed for the fixed-point theorem.

statement: Let $C\subseteq A^n$ be a [code](c:error-correcting-code) with $M\ge2$ words over an alphabet of $q$ symbols, with minimum Hamming distance $d$. Put $\theta=(q-1)/q$. If $d>\theta n$, then $M\le d/(d-\theta n)$.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet has $q\ge2$ symbols.
Distinct codewords of the [code](c:error-correcting-code) have Hamming distance at least $d$.
The bound $d>\theta n$ holds, so the right side is positive and finite.

conclusion: The number of codewords satisfies $M\le d/(d-\theta n)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only that Hamming distance is symmetric. The Plotkin bound is stated here.

proofs.name: Count the sum of distances twice
proofs.slogan: Bound the sum of all pairwise distances from below by $d$ and from above by a coordinate count.
proofs.scope: The whole bound for every alphabet size $q\ge2$. The proof is a double count of ordered pairs.

roles.why: The alphabet size gives the Cauchy-Schwarz factor $q$ in each coordinate.
The minimum distance gives the lower bound on the sum of distances.
The positive gap lets the last step divide by $d-\theta n$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum of ordered-pair distances from below.
steps.detail: Let $S$ be the sum of $d(x,y)$ over ordered pairs of distinct codewords. There are $M(M-1)$ such pairs, each with distance at least $d$. So $S\ge M(M-1)d$.

steps.slogan: Split $S$ by coordinate.
steps.detail: The distance $d(x,y)$ counts the coordinates $i$ with $x_i\ne y_i$. So $S=\sum_{i=1}^nS_i$, where $S_i$ counts ordered pairs of codewords that differ at coordinate $i$.

steps.slogan: Count the pairs that agree at a coordinate.
steps.detail: Fix $i$. Let $m_a$ be the number of codewords with symbol $a$ at coordinate $i$, so $\sum_am_a=M$. The ordered pairs that agree number $\sum_am_a^2$. So $S_i=M^2-\sum_am_a^2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the squares from below by Cauchy-Schwarz.
steps.detail: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for $(m_a)$ and the all-ones vector in $\mathbb R^q$ gives $M^2\le q\sum_am_a^2$. So $S_i\le M^2-M^2/q=\theta M^2$, and $S\le\theta nM^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two bounds and divide.
steps.detail: We get $M(M-1)d\le\theta nM^2$, so $(M-1)d\le\theta nM$, which is $M(d-\theta n)\le d$. Divide by $d-\theta n>0$.

concepts.c:error-correcting-code: The theorem bounds the size of a code from its minimum distance.

statement: Let a group $G$ be covered by $n$ left [cosets](c:coset) $g_iH_i$. Then some $H_i$ has finite [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup). The cosets with finite index already cover $G$, and $\sum 1/[G:H_i]\ge1$ over those. In particular some $[G:H_i]\le n$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is any group. It may be infinite and non-abelian.
The family of [cosets](c:coset) is finite with $n\ge1$ members, and repeated subgroups are allowed.
The additive form for abelian groups is the same statement.

conclusion: A finite coset cover has a member of finite index at most $n$, the finite-index members cover $G$, and their reciprocal indices sum to at least $1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the existence of a member of index at most the cardinality of the cover. The covering by finite-index members and the sum inequality are stated here.

proofs.name: Induction on the number of distinct subgroups
proofs.slogan: Remove one subgroup at a time by induction, then count cosets of the common subgroup of finite-index members.
proofs.scope: The full statement (a) to (d) for every group and every finite cover.

roles.why: The group is arbitrary, so the induction works for every group.
The cover is finite, so the intersection of finite-index members has finite index.
The additive form follows by the same proof in an abelian group, so it is not used here.

steps.slogan: Start an induction on the number of distinct subgroups.
steps.detail: Claim: a cover that uses at most $m$ distinct subgroups has a member of finite index. For $m=0$ the union is empty, which is impossible. For the step fix a member subgroup $H$. If the cosets of $H$ in the cover cover $G$, then $H$ has finite index and we are done.

steps.slogan: Replace the cosets of $H$ by cosets of the other subgroups.
steps.detail: Otherwise some coset $xH$ is not in the cover. For $z\in yH$, $xy^{-1}z\in xH$ lies in a member $g_iH_i$ with $H_i\ne H$, so $z\in(yx^{-1}g_i)H_i$. So a cover with at most $m-1$ subgroups exists. By induction one of the $H_i$ has finite index.

steps.slogan: Show that the finite-index members already cover.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be the set of $i$ with $[G:H_i]$ finite, and $D=\bigcap_{i\in F}H_i$. Then $[G:D]$ is finite and each $g_iH_i$ with $i\in F$ is a union of cosets of $D$. If these cosets did not cover $G$, the argument of step 2 with $H=D$ would give a cover by infinite-index subgroups only. This contradicts the first claim.

steps.slogan: Count the cosets of $D$ to get the sum inequality.
steps.detail: $G$ has $[G:D]$ cosets of $D$, and each lies in some $g_iH_i$ with $i\in F$, which holds $[H_i:D]$ of them. So $[G:D]\le\sum_{F}[H_i:D]$. Divide by $[G:D]=[G:H_i][H_i:D]$ to get $1\le\sum_{F}1/[G:H_i]$.

steps.slogan: Deduce a member of index at most $n$.
steps.detail: Suppose $[G:H_i]>n$ for every finite-index $H_i$. Then each term of the sum is less than $1/n$, and the other terms are $0<1/n$. The sum of $n$ terms is less than $1$. This contradicts step 4.

concepts.c:coset: The cover uses cosets, and the proof counts cosets of the common subgroup.
concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: Finite index is what the induction finds and the sum bounds.

statement: Let $G$ be a group whose [center](c:center) $Z$ has finite [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $n$. Then $g\mapsto g^n$ is a group homomorphism $G\to Z$, the [transfer homomorphism](c:transfer-homomorphism). Every element of the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) $G'$ satisfies $g^n=1$. Moreover $G'$ is finite.

hypotheses.text: The subgroup $Z$ is the [center](c:center) of $G$.
The [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $n=[G:Z]$ is finite and at least $1$.
The group $G$ may be infinite, and $G'$ is generated by all commutators $[x,y]$.

conclusion: The map $g\mapsto g^n$ is a homomorphism into $Z$, it kills $G'$, and $G'$ is finite.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the transfer to the center is the $n$-th power map. The finiteness of $G'$ and the exponent of $G'$ are stated here.

proofs.name: Transfer to the center
proofs.slogan: Show that the transfer to the center is the power map, then bound the commutators and use Schreier.
proofs.scope: The full statement for every group with $[G:Z]=n<\infty$.

roles.why: Centrality makes the transfer product multiplicative and makes commutators depend only on cosets.
Finite index gives a finite transversal, at most $n^2$ commutators, and the exponent $n$.
The subgroup $G'$ lies in the kernel of the map to the abelian group $Z$, and it is the group to bound.

steps.slogan: Define the transfer and prove it is a homomorphism.
steps.detail: Choose coset representatives $t_1,\dots,t_n$ of $Z$. Write $g\,t_i=t_{\sigma_g(i)}z_i(g)$ with $z_i(g)\in Z$. Because $Z$ is central and abelian, $V(g)=\prod_iz_i(g)$ satisfies $V(gh)=V(g)V(h)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $V(g)=g^n$ by splitting into cycles.
steps.detail: Split $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into cycles of $\sigma_g$. For a cycle of length $m$, $g^mt_{i_1}=t_{i_1}z_{i_1}(g)\cdots z_{i_m}(g)$, and the product is central. So $g^m$ equals that product. Multiplying over the cycles gives $V(g)=g^n$ because the lengths add up to $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that every commutator has order dividing $n$.
steps.detail: The target $Z$ is abelian, so $G'$ lies in the kernel of $V$. Hence $g^n=1$ for all $g\in G'$.

steps.slogan: Bound the number of commutators by $n^2$.
steps.detail: For central $z,w$, $[xz,yw]=[x,y]$. So $[x,y]$ depends only on the cosets $xZ$ and $yZ$, and there are at most $n^2$ commutators. So $G'$ is generated by at most $n^2$ elements.

steps.slogan: Apply the Schreier lemma to bound $G'\cap Z$ and $G'$.
steps.detail: The index $[G':G'\cap Z]$ is at most $n$, because $G'/(G'\cap Z)$ embeds in $G/Z$. By Schreier's lemma, $G'\cap Z$ is generated by at most $n^3$ elements. It is abelian of exponent dividing $n$, so it is finite. Hence $G'$ is finite.

concepts.c:center: Central elements make the transfer multiplicative and commutators depend only on cosets.
concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: The finite index $n$ bounds the cosets, the commutators and the exponent.
concepts.c:transfer-homomorphism: The transfer to the center becomes the $n$-th power map.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: It is the subgroup shown to be finite of exponent dividing $n$.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $D(f)$ the [basic open set](c:basic-open) of the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum). Then $D(f)=\emptyset$ iff $f$ is nilpotent. Also $D(f)\subseteq\bigcup D(f_i)$ iff $f$ lies in the radical of $(f_i)$, and then finitely many $f_i$ suffice. Every $D(f)$ and Spec $R$ itself are [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact).

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative with $1$, and its [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) is empty if $R=0$.
The prime spectrum carries the [Zariski topology](c:zariski-topology), with closed sets $V(I)$.
The theorem does not claim that every open set is [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact).

conclusion: The set $D(f)$ is empty iff $f$ is nilpotent, covers by basic opens reduce to the radical, and every basic open set and Spec $R$ is quasi-compact.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a basic open set is compact. The criteria for emptiness and for covers are stated here.

proofs.name: Radical of the generated ideal
proofs.slogan: Turn a cover of $D(f)$ into a statement about the radical of an ideal, then use finite generation.
proofs.scope: All commutative rings, including $R=0$.

roles.why: Maximal ideals exist in a nonzero ring, and the nilradical is the intersection of the primes.
The closed sets $V(I)$ turn covers into containments of closed sets.
This hypothesis is a warning only. The proof treats basic open sets, so it is not used.

steps.slogan: Prove the two criteria for $D(f)$.
steps.detail: $D(f)=\emptyset$ iff $f$ lies in every prime, iff $f$ is in the [nilradical](c:nilradical), iff $f$ is nilpotent. If $f$ is a unit, no prime contains $f$. If $f$ is not a unit, $(f)$ lies in a maximal ideal, which is prime, so $D(f)\ne\operatorname{Spec}R$.

steps.slogan: Take complements of a cover.
steps.detail: Let $I=(f_i)$. A prime lies outside $\bigcup D(f_i)$ iff it contains $I$, and outside $D(f)$ iff it contains $f$. So $D(f)\subseteq\bigcup D(f_i)$ iff $V(I)\subseteq V(f)$.

steps.slogan: Read the containment as membership in the radical.
steps.detail: $V(I)\subseteq V(f)$ says that $f$ lies in every prime containing $I$. The primes of $R/I$ are these primes, so the nilradical result for $R/I$ shows that this holds iff $f\in\sqrt I$.

steps.slogan: Extract a finite subfamily.
steps.detail: If $f\in\sqrt I$, then $f^N\in I$ for some $N$. An element of $I$ is a finite combination $\sum_{i\in F}a_if_i$. So $f^N\in(f_i:i\in F)$, and the equivalence above gives $D(f)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in F}D(f_i)$.

steps.slogan: Reduce an open cover to basic opens and conclude.
steps.detail: Cover $D(f)$ by open sets $U_j$. The basic open sets inside some $U_j$ cover $D(f)$. By the finite step, finitely many of them cover $D(f)$, so finitely many $U_j$ do. Since Spec $R=D(1)$, it is quasi-compact too.

steps.slogan: Collect the criteria and the compactness.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives part (a). Steps 2 to 4 give part (b). Step 5 gives part (c).

concepts.c:prime-spectrum: It is the space on which all the statements live.
concepts.c:quasi-compact: Finite subcovers are the goal of the last step.
concepts.c:zariski-topology: Closed sets $V(I)$ turn covers into containments.
concepts.c:nilradical: It is the intersection of all primes and identifies empty basic opens.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For each [idempotent](c:idempotent) $e$, the [basic open set](c:basic-open) $D(e)$ is [clopen](c:clopen-subset), with complement $D(1-e)$. Every clopen subset of the [prime spectrum](c:prime-spectrum) equals $D(e)$ for exactly one idempotent $e$. So $e\mapsto D(e)$ is a bijection from idempotents to clopen subsets.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative with $1$, and $R=0$ is allowed.
The prime spectrum carries the Zariski topology with closed sets $V(I)$.

conclusion: The map $e\mapsto D(e)$ is a bijection from the idempotents of $R$ to the clopen subsets of Spec $R$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a basic open set is clopen under a related product-and-sum condition. The bijection with all clopen subsets is stated here.

proofs.name: Comaximal ideals with nilpotent product
proofs.slogan: Split a clopen set into two closed sets, use quasi-compactness, then build the idempotent.
proofs.scope: All commutative rings. For $R=0$ both sides are the single empty set.

roles.why: Idempotents and nilpotents in a commutative ring behave as in the steps, and $1=e+(1-e)$.
The topology gives the closed sets $V(I)$ and quasi-compactness of closed sets.

steps.slogan: Show that $D(e)$ is clopen.
steps.detail: If $e^2=e$, then $e(1-e)=0$ and $e+(1-e)=1$. A prime contains exactly one of $e$ and $1-e$. So Spec $R$ is the disjoint union of the open sets $D(e)$ and $D(1-e)$.

steps.detail:
If $P\in U=V(I')$, then $i\in P$, so $j

steps.slogan: Collect the three parts of the bijection.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that the map lands in clopen sets. Step 2 shows that it is injective. Step 6 shows that it is onto.

statement: Let $\pi_k$ be the monic [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) polynomials of a weight $w$, with $x\pi_k=\pi_{k+1}+\alpha_k\pi_k+\beta_k\pi_{k-1}$. The Jacobi matrix $J_n$ is a [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix) with $\det(xI-J_n)=\pi_n$. So its [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) are the Gauss nodes, and the Gauss weight at a node is $\int w$ times the squared first entry of a unit [eigenvector](c:eigenvector).

hypotheses.text: The weight satisfies the hypotheses of Gauss quadrature, so $\pi_k$ exists and $h_k>0$.
The size $n\ge1$, and the [characteristic polynomial](c:characteristic-polynomial) of $J_n$ is monic of degree $n$.
Eigenvectors are taken in $\mathbb R^n$ with the standard inner product.

conclusion: Orthogonal polynomials satisfy a three-term recurrence, the eigenvalues of $J_n$ are the Gauss nodes, and the Gauss weights come from the first entries of unit eigenvectors.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the real spectrum of a self-adjoint operator is the range of its eigenvalues. The recurrence, the determinant identity and the weight formula are stated here.

proofs.name: Recurrence, determinant and eigenvector
proofs.slogan: Derive the recurrence, match it with a determinant recurrence, then read the nodes and weights.
proofs.scope: The three parts for each $n\ge1$. Real and simple roots come from the Gauss quadrature theorem.

roles.why: The weight defines the inner product, so multiplication by $x$ is symmetric and $h_k>0$.
The determinant of $xI-J_n$ is the monic polynomial compared with $\pi_n$.
Unit eigenvectors in $\mathbb R^n$ give the squared first entry.

steps.slogan: Derive the three-term recurrence.
steps.detail: $\langle xf,g\rangle=\langle f,xg\rangle$. Expand $x\pi_k-\pi_{k+1}$ in $\pi_0,\dots,\pi_k$. The coefficient of $\pi_j$ is $\langle x\pi_k,\pi_j\rangle/h_j$, which is $0$ for $j<k-1$, is $\alpha_k$ for $j=k$, and is $h_k/h_{k-1}=\beta_k$ for $j=k-1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the characteristic polynomials satisfy the same recurrence.
steps.detail: Expand $D_{k+1}=\det(xI-J_{k+1})$ along the last row to get $D_{k+1}=(x-\alpha_k)D_k-\beta_kD_{k-1}$. With $D_0=1=\pi_0$ and $D_1=\pi_1$, induction gives $D_k=\pi_k$. So $\det(xI-J_n)=\pi_n$, and the eigenvalues are the nodes.

steps.slogan: Build an eigenvector from the orthonormal polynomials.
steps.detail: Divide the recurrence by $\sqrt{h_k}$ to get $xp_k=\sqrt{\beta_{k+1}}p_{k+1}+\alpha_kp_k+\sqrt{\beta_k}p_{k-1}$. Let $P(x)=(p_0,\dots,p_{n-1})^T$. At a root $x_i$ of $\pi_n$, $p_n(x_i)=0$, so $J_nP(x_i)=x_iP(x_i)$. Its first entry is $h_0^{-1/2}\ne0$.

steps.slogan: Normalize the eigenvector to unit length.
steps.detail: The eigenvalue $x_i$ is simple, so the eigenspace is spanned by $P(x_i)$. The unit vector has $v_{i,1}^2=h_0^{-1}/\sum_kp_k(x_i)^2$.

steps.slogan: Find the Christoffel formula for the weights.
steps.detail: Expand the Lagrange polynomial $\ell_i$ in $p_0,\dots,p_{n-1}$. Exactness of the Gauss rule for degree $2n-2$ gives the coefficients $\lambda_ip_k(x_i)$. Evaluating at $x_i$ gives $\lambda_i=1/\sum_kp_k(x_i)^2$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two formulas for the weight.
steps.detail: Steps 4 and 5 give two formulas for the weight, $\lambda_i=1/\sum p_k(x_i)^2$ and $\lambda_i=h_0v_{i,1}^2$. Here $h_0=\int w$.

concepts.c:symmetric-matrix: The Jacobi matrix is symmetric, so it has real eigenvalues.

concepts.c:eigenvector: The weights come from the first entries of unit eigenvectors.

statement: Let $f$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a,b]$ and $p$ a real [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree at most $n$, with $e=f-p$. Take $n+2$ points $t_0<\dots<t_{n+1}$ where $e(t_i)$ is nonzero with alternating signs. Then every polynomial $q$ of degree at most $n$ has $\max|f-q|\ge\min|e(t_i)|$. If also $|e(t_i)|=\max|e|$, then $p$ is the unique [best approximation](c:best-approximation).

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is real and [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed interval $[a,b]$.
The functions $p$ and $q$ are real [polynomials](c:polynomial) of degree at most $n$.
The points $t_0<\dots<t_{n+1}$ are $n+2$ distinct points of $[a,b]$.

conclusion: Alternating errors give a lower bound for every competitor, and equioscillation at maximal error makes $p$ the unique best uniform approximation.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a nonzero polynomial has at most as many roots as its degree. The alternation bound and the uniqueness claim are stated here.

proofs.name: Divided differences and alternating signs
proofs.slogan: Use the vanishing divided difference of a polynomial of degree at most $n$ on $n+2$ nodes, and compare signs.
proofs.scope: Parts (a) and (b), for every $n\ge0$ and every interval $[a,b]$.

roles.why: Continuity makes the maximum of $|e|$ exist, so equioscillation at the maximum is meaningful.
Degree at most $n$ makes $r=p-q$ have vanishing divided difference on $n+2$ nodes.
The $n+2$ nodes carry the alternating signs and the identity.

steps.slogan: Find the signs of the node weights.
steps.detail: Put $w(x)=\prod_j(x-t_j)$ and $w_i=w'(t_i)$. Exactly $n+1-i$ factors of $w_i$ are negative, so $\operatorname{sign}w_i=(-1)^{n+1-i}$.

steps.slogan: Prove the identity $\sum r(t_i)/w_i=0$ for degree at most $n$.
steps.detail: The interpolating polynomial of degree at most $n+1$ at the $n+2$ nodes is unique, and Lagrange gives it as $\sum r(t_i)\prod_{j\ne i}(x-t_j)/w_i$. The polynomial $r$ itself interpolates. The coefficient of $x^{n+1}$ is $0$ on the left and $\sum r(t_i)/w_i$ on the right.

steps.slogan: Prove the lower bound (a) by contradiction.
steps.detail: Suppose $\max|f-q|<\lambda=\min|e(t_i)|$ and put $r=p-q$. At each node $r(t_i)$ has the sign of $-e(t_i)$. Then the terms $r(t_i)/w_i$ have one common nonzero sign, so their sum is nonzero. This contradicts the identity.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ is a best approximation.
steps.detail: If $|e(t_i)|=E=\max|e|$, part (a) gives $\max|f-q|\ge E=\max|f-p|$ for every $q$. So no polynomial of degree at most $n$ has a smaller maximal error than $p$.

steps.slogan: Show that a second best approximation equals $p$.
steps.detail: Let $\max|f-q|=E$ and $r=p-q$. At the nodes, $s(-1)^ir(t_i)\le0$. So all terms $r(t_i)/w_i$ have the same weak sign, and their sum is $0$ by the identity. Hence $r(t_i)=0$ at $n+2$ nodes. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n$ has at most $n$ roots, so $r=0$.

steps.slogan: Collect the lower bound and the uniqueness.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives part (a). Steps 4 and 5 give part (b).

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity makes the maximum error exist.
concepts.c:polynomial: Degree at most $n$ makes the divided difference vanish.
concepts.c:best-approximation: The theorem identifies the unique best uniform approximation.

statement: Let $X$ be a [finite set](c:finite-set) and $f\colon X\to\mathbb R^k$. Let $p^*(x)\propto e^{-\beta\cdot f(x)}$ be the [Gibbs distribution](c:gibbs-distribution) with mean $m$ of $f$. For every [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $q$ with the same mean, $H(q)=H(p^*)-D(q\|p^*)$. So $H(q)\le H(p^*)$, with equality iff $q=p^*$.

hypotheses.text: The set $X$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set) and $f$ takes real values.
The competitor $q$ is a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) with the same mean of $f$ as $p^*$.
Every $p^*(x)$ is strictly positive, so $D(q\|p^*)$ is finite.

conclusion: The entropy of $q$ is the entropy of $p^*$ minus the divergence, so $p^*$ is the unique maximizer of entropy with the mean constraint.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the divergence is zero iff the two measures are equal. The entropy identity and the maximum are stated here.

proofs.name: Log of the Gibbs law is affine
proofs.slogan: Use that the log of the Gibbs law is affine in $f$, so the cross term depends only on the mean.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, including $k=0$, where $p^*$ is uniform.

roles.why: Finiteness makes all sums finite and the entropy well defined.
The equal mean makes the cross term the same for $q$ and $p^*$.
Positivity makes $\log p^*$ finite and the divergence finite.

steps.slogan: Show that $\log p^*$ is affine in $f$.
steps.detail: Since $p^*(x)=e^{-\beta\cdot f(x)}/Z>0$, $\log p^*(x)=-\beta\cdot f(x)-\log Z$. So for any $q$, $-\sum_xq\log p^*=\beta\cdot\sum_xqf+\log Z$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the cross term for $p^*$ and for $q$.
steps.detail: For $q=p^*$ we get $H(p^*)=\beta\cdot m+\log Z$. If $q$ has mean $m$, the cross term $-\sum q\log p^*$ is the same number $H(p^*)$.

steps.slogan: Expand the divergence into entropy terms.
steps.detail: $D(q\|p^*)=\sum q\log q-\sum q\log p^*=-H(q)+H(p^*)$. This is the identity $H(q)=H(p^*)-D(q\|p^*)$, because the cross term equals $H(p^*)$ by step 2.

steps.slogan: Apply nonnegativity of the divergence.
steps.detail: Gibbs' inequality gives $D(q\|p^*)\ge0$ with equality iff $q=p^*$. So $H(q)\le H(p^*)$, with equality only for $q=p^*$.

steps.slogan: Read the case without constraints.
steps.detail: For $k=0$ or $\beta=0$, $Z=|X|$ and $p^*$ is uniform. So $H(q)=\log|X|-D(q\|u)\le\log|X|$, with equality only for the uniform law.

concepts.c:gibbs-distribution: Its log is affine in $f$, which makes the identity work.
concepts.c:probability-distribution: The competitor $q$ ranges over probability distributions with the same mean.

statement: Let $A\ne0$ be a complex [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) with unit of norm $1$, and $a\in A$. Then the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) $\sigma(a)$ is a compact subset of $\{|\lambda|\le\|a\|\}$. The [resolvent](c:resolvent) $R(\lambda)=(\lambda-a)^{-1}$ satisfies $R(\lambda)-R(\mu)=(\mu-\lambda)R(\lambda)R(\mu)$ and is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) with $R'=-R^2$. Also $\sigma(a)\ne\emptyset$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $A$ is complete for a submultiplicative norm, so $\|xy\|\le\|x\|\|y\|$.
The scalar field is $\mathbb C$, the unit has norm $1$ and $1\ne0$.
The algebra $A$ need not be commutative.

conclusion: The spectrum is compact and nonempty, and the resolvent obeys the resolvent identity and is holomorphic with the stated bounds.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the spectrum of an element of a complex Banach algebra is nonempty. The compactness, the resolvent identity and the bounds are stated here.

proofs.name: Neumann series and Liouville
proofs.slogan: Build the resolvent from Neumann series, then use Liouville and Hahn-Banach to exclude an empty spectrum.
proofs.scope: All five parts. The scalar field must be $\mathbb C$, because part (v) is false over $\mathbb R$.

roles.why: Submultiplicativity and completeness make the Neumann series converge.
Complex scalars allow Liouville's theorem, and norm $1$ of the unit gives the series bound.
The proof uses only powers of one element, so it never needs commutativity.

steps.slogan: Sum the Neumann series.
steps.detail: If $\|x\|<1$, then $\|x^n\|\le\|x\|^n$, so $\sum x^n$ converges in the complete algebra to an inverse of $1-x$, with norm at most $1/(1-\|x\|)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the resolvent outside the disc.
steps.detail: For $|\lambda|>\|a\|$, write $\lambda-a=\lambda(1-a/\lambda)$. Step 1 gives invertibility and $\|R(\lambda)\|\le1/(|\lambda|-\|a\|)$. So $\sigma(a)\subseteq\{|\lambda|\le\|a\|\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the resolvent set is open and give the power series.
steps.detail: For $\lambda_0\in\rho(a)$ and $|\lambda-\lambda_0|<1/\|R(\lambda_0)\|$, step 1 gives $R(\lambda)=\sum(-1)^n(\lambda-\lambda_0)^nR(\lambda_0)^{n+1}$. So $\rho(a)$ is open, $\sigma(a)$ is compact, and $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda_0,\sigma(a))\ge1/\|R(\lambda_0)\|$.

steps.slogan: Prove the resolvent identity and holomorphy.
steps.detail: $R(\lambda)-R(\mu)=R(\lambda)[(\mu-a)-(\lambda-a)]R(\mu)=(\mu-\lambda)R(\lambda)R(\mu)$. The linear coefficient of the series is $-R(\lambda_0)^2$, so $R$ is holomorphic with $R'=-R^2$.

steps.slogan: Assume an empty spectrum and apply Liouville.
steps.detail: Let $\sigma(a)=\emptyset$ and let $\varphi$ be a bounded linear functional. Then $f=\varphi\circ R$ is entire, bounded and tends to $0$ at infinity. By Liouville's theorem $f\equiv0$.

steps.slogan: Reach a contradiction with Hahn-Banach.
steps.detail: Step 5 gives $\varphi(R(0))=0$ for every bounded $\varphi$. By the Hahn-Banach theorem, $R(0)=0$. But $R(0)(-a)=1\ne0$. So $\sigma(a)\ne\emptyset$.

concepts.c:banach-algebra: Completeness and submultiplicativity make the Neumann series converge.
concepts.c:spectrum-of-an-operator: The spectrum is the set shown compact and nonempty.
concepts.c:resolvent: The resolvent is the holomorphic function studied.
concepts.c:norm: The norm bounds the Neumann series.

statement: For $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ let $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx$ be the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform). If $f,f',\dots,f^{(m)}$ are [integrable](c:lebesgue-integral), then $\widehat{f^{(j)}}=(2\pi i\xi)^j\hat f$, so $|\xi|^m\hat f(\xi)\to0$. If $x^jf$ is integrable for $j\le m$, then $\hat f\in C^m$ and $\hat f^{(j)}=\widehat{(-2\pi ix)^jf}$.

hypotheses.text: In part (A) the [derivatives](c:derivative) $f^{(j)}$ are classical, continuous and integrable.
In part (B) the functions $x^jf$ are integrable, not only $f$.
The convention of the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) has the factor $2\pi$ in the exponent.

conclusion: Derivatives of $f$ become multiplication by $2\pi i\xi$ and give decay of $\hat f$. Multiplication by $x$ becomes differentiation of $\hat f$ and gives smoothness.

formal.difference: The declaration states the derivative rule of the Fourier integral in a related form. The decay claim and the smoothness claim are stated here.

proofs.name: Integrate by parts and differentiate under the integral
proofs.slogan: Trade derivatives for multipliers by integration by parts, and multipliers for derivatives by dominated convergence.
proofs.scope: Parts (A) and (B) on the real line. The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma is cited.

roles.why: Integrable continuous derivatives let the boundary terms vanish and give the decay bound.
Integrability of $x^jf$ gives the dominating function for differentiation.
The factor $2\pi$ in the exponent produces the multiplier $2\pi i\xi$.

steps.slogan: Show that the boundary values vanish.
steps.detail: If $g,g'\in L^1$ with $g$ continuous, $g(x)=g(0)+\int_0^xg'$ has limits at $\pm\infty$. Since $g$ is integrable, both limits are $0$. Apply this to $g=f^{(j)}$ for $j<m$.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts and iterate.
steps.detail: On $[-R,R]$, $\int f^{(j+1)}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx$ equals a boundary term plus $2\pi i\xi\int f^{(j)}e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx$. Let $R\to\infty$. The boundary term vanishes, so $\widehat{f^{(j+1)}}=2\pi i\xi\widehat{f^{(j)}}$. By induction $\widehat{f^{(j)}}=(2\pi i\xi)^j\hat f$.

steps.slogan: Bound and decay of $\hat f$.
steps.detail: By step 2, $|2\pi\xi|^m|\hat f(\xi)|=|\widehat{f^{(m)}}(\xi)|\le\|f^{(m)}\|_1$. The Riemann-Lebesgue lemma gives $\widehat{f^{(m)}}(\xi)\to0$, so $|\xi|^m\hat f(\xi)\to0$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate under the integral once.
steps.detail: If $xf\in L^1$, the difference quotient $\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}(e^{-2\pi ixh}-1)/h\,dx$ has integrand bounded by $2\pi|x||f(x)|$ and tends to $-2\pi ixf(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}$. Dominated convergence gives $\hat f'(\xi)=\int(-2\pi ix)f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx$.

steps.slogan: Repeat for higher derivatives.
steps.detail: Apply step 4 to $(-2\pi ix)^jf$ for $j<m$. Each $\hat f^{(j)}$ is continuous, again by dominated convergence. So $\hat f\in C^m$.

steps.slogan: Collect the parts (A) and (B).
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 give part (A). Steps 4 and 5 give part (B).

concepts.c:derivative: Derivatives of $f$ become multipliers of $\hat f$.
